repository.title: HelioForge Hybrid Energy Lab
repository.description: Explore hybrid-energy assumptions, storage dispatch & auditable numerical screens using a reproducible Python workbench.
repository.summary: The source combines a hybrid adequacy screen, storage MILP, research studies, and an interactive learning workbench. The companion starts with a small synthetic daily power balance.
repository.audience: Energy researchers, engineering educators, and developers inspecting hybrid-resource assumptions.

model.equation: solar = S · max(0, sin(π(t−6)/12)); demand = D · (0.8 + 0.18 cos(2π(t−19)/24) + 0.12 exp(−((t−19)/3)²)); import = max(demand−solar−battery, 0).
assumptions: An idealized clear-day profile represents one 24-hour period.
Battery discharge is a fixed external power contribution; energy inventory and charge scheduling are omitted.
Solar share is capped at 100%; exports are not credited; grid carbon intensity is constant.
The native greedy hourly hybrid screen and storage MILP are different algorithms; this browser proxy executes neither.
PV and load profiles are invented and repeatable. No current weather, tariff, irradiance service, or device connector is active.
The fixed battery contribution has no capacity state, so lower import cannot prove outage adequacy or an optimized dispatch.
model.introduction: A simple solar-demand-battery contribution illustrates the accounting questions asked by the native workbench. It omits the native hybrid inventory rules, backup sequence, and separate storage optimization.

modules.title: Follow a single-bus balance
modules.objective: Identify which sources serve demand and where a simple screen stops.
steps: Read the scope and hourly units in docs/HYBRID_METHODOLOGY.md.
Apply 500 kW demand baseline, 600 kW PV peak, and zero battery contribution.
Compare noon with 19:00 and explain why a surplus at one hour does not automatically serve another.
modules.reflection: Which native state and efficiency terms are needed to move surplus energy from noon to evening?

modules.title: Test a resource sensitivity
modules.objective: Quantify the effect of a smaller solar resource without changing demand.
steps: Keep baseline demand fixed and reduce PV peak from 600 to 300 kW.
Predict whether noon imports become positive, then run the scenario.
Compare the constant clear-day shape with the source’s declared synthetic hourly profiles.

checkpoints.label: Noon grid import under reduced PV

modules.reflection: Why would a result based on this profile need measured or sourced weather and load data before a site-specific study?

modules.title: Separate adequacy from optimization
modules.objective: Explain the different questions answered by a dispatch policy and a cost-minimizing storage model.
steps: Raise demand to 800 kW, use a 400 kW PV peak, and add an assumed 100 kW battery contribution.
Inspect the evening import and emissions rate in the stress case.
Read the native hybrid-policy order and the storage MILP objective; identify their different terminal-inventory conventions.
modules.reflection: What inventory, power-direction, price, and terminal-state constraints would be required to call a schedule optimized?

modules.title: Prepare a reproducible native follow-up
modules.objective: Carry a transparent screening question into the source workbench without inflating the claim.
steps: Use 500 kW demand, 300 kW PV, 200 kW assumed battery discharge, and 200 g/kWh grid carbon.
Run and export the scenario, noting the missing battery-energy state.
Follow START_HERE.md to identify the local API route for a real native hybrid calculation and record its source revision and assumptions.
modules.reflection: Which findings would remain an adequacy screen, and which additional evidence would be required for finance, stability, or plant control?

source.scope: This browser lab is a standalone teaching approximation. Use the linked source for the project implementation.
